cash-advance-fee.exampleNote: Original scenarios checked against independent 70-digit Python Decimal calculations. This verifies arithmetic for the stated assumptions, not a card agreement, COBRA eligibility or external professional review.

sections.title: How does a $53 fee become a $77.66 cost?
paragraphs: Simple interest on $1,000 for 30 days at 30% / 365 is about $24.66.
Cost is about $77.66; principal plus cost is about $1,077.66.
sections.formula: Fee = max(amount × fee rate, minimum) + ATM; simple interest = selected balance × APR / day basis × days.

sections.title: What changes when the fees are financed?
paragraphs: With all $53 of fees financed, the starting balance is $1,053. The same 30-day simple-interest assumption gives about $25.96 in interest and $78.96 in cost. The fees are counted once in that cost, not once at withdrawal and again in repayment.
Fee-specific agreements can differ. The worksheet applies the selected treatment to both fees; it does not infer an issuer’s rules.

sections.title: What does paying earlier change?
paragraphs: At 7, 14 and 30 days with separately paid fees, the $53 upfront charge is unchanged. Only the interest varies in this comparison. The table assumes no partial payments.
Interest usually starts at the cash advance transaction date. Check the actual posting and accrual rules; selecting zero days is a mathematical fee-only boundary.

sections.title: Why is simple annualized cost different from APR?
paragraphs: Dividing cost by cash received and scaling by days per year is only a simple annualized comparison. It does not solve the yield of a dated cash-flow stream or establish a legally disclosed APR.

Daily compound is an explicitly selectable approximation. A statement-based or monthly-capitalization process can produce a different bill. There are no lender-specific rates or approved financing alternatives supplied by this tool.

questions.question: Does the minimum fee replace the percentage fee?
questions.answer: The advance fee is the larger of the entered percentage charge and minimum fee, then the additional ATM fee is added once.

questions.question: Do the fees themselves accrue interest?
questions.answer: That depends on the agreement. Choose separately paid fees or add both entered fees to the interest-bearing starting balance. Different fee-specific treatment requires a separate calculation.

questions.question: Is the annualized cost an APR quote?
questions.answer: No. It is a simple annualization of the modeled cost relative to cash received. It is not a statutory APR, IRR or effective annual yield, and zero days gives no annualized value.

questions.question: Is the table a minimum-payment schedule?
questions.answer: No. Each row assumes one full repayment on that day and no earlier payment. Use a payoff tool separately for installment budgeting; its rate and balance assumptions must match.

sources.title: CFPB: Credit-card grace periods
sources.usedFor: Cash advances generally start accruing interest at the transaction date.
sources.scope: Background only; card-specific fees, interest-bearing balances and compounding must come from the user agreement. No source endorses this calculator.

presets.label: Pay fees separately and repay after 30 days
Finance fees on the same advance
Compare daily compounding with simple interest
Zero days isolates the upfront fees

limitations: One USD credit-card cash advance with a single full repayment, selected daily simple or compounded interest, explicit day basis and fee treatment. No intervening payments, statement-cycle capitalization, purchase balances, issuer quote, statutory APR or merchant cash advance.

cobra-cost.answer: COBRA premium planning starts with the full plan cost, including the employer contribution. With $200 from the employee, $600 from the employer and a selected 2% administrative charge, the monthly amount is $816 before any entered subsidy. This worksheet estimates premiums, not eligibility or total medical spending.
cobra-cost.exampleNote: Original scenarios checked against independent 70-digit Python Decimal calculations. This verifies arithmetic for the stated assumptions, not a card agreement, COBRA eligibility or external professional review.

sections.title: Why can an $200 payroll amount become an $816 premium?
paragraphs: Monthly amount is $816, or $4,896 over six selected months.
sections.formula: Full premium = employee share + employer share. Modeled monthly payment = full premium × (1 + administrative rate) − entered subsidy.

sections.title: What if I already know the full plan cost?
paragraphs: Use Known Full Plan Premium mode and enter $800 directly. The previous $200 employee payment is only a comparison baseline and is not added to the premium again.
Use the same coverage tier and monthly frequency. Family coverage and employee-only coverage are not interchangeable inputs.

sections.title: How should temporary employer assistance be modeled?
paragraphs: An entered $300 subsidy reduces the $816 payment to $516. Over six months at the unchanged subsidy, payments total $3,096.
If support ends earlier, run separate periods. For three supported months and three unsupported months, the total is 3 × $516 + 3 × $816 = $3,996. No assistance program is assumed automatically.

sections.title: What does the standard 102% limit leave out?
paragraphs: The ordinary federal rule permits a charge up to 102% of the applicable plan cost; an entered 0% administrative charge is also possible. The default 2% is illustrative and not an assertion that every plan charges it.

Certain disability-extension months can have different limits, including up to 150%. This worksheet does not model that extension, state continuation or eligibility. Selected planning months do not establish entitlement to coverage.
Compare medical deductibles, provider networks and other costs separately. This premium worksheet does not estimate ACA subsidies, after-tax effects or recommend which coverage to choose.

questions.question: Do I multiply just my old payroll deduction by 1.02?
questions.answer: No. Start with the full plan cost for the same coverage tier, including the amount the employer used to contribute. The ordinary administrative charge can be up to 2%.

questions.question: Does choosing 18 or 36 months mean I qualify?
questions.answer: No. The month input only controls arithmetic. Eligibility, election deadlines, qualifying events and permitted duration require the plan notice and applicable rules.

questions.question: What if the subsidy ends after three months?
questions.answer: Run the subsidized months and remaining unsubsidized months separately, then add the two amounts. This worksheet applies one unchanged subsidy to each selected month.

questions.question: Does this estimate include deductibles or the disability extension?
questions.answer: No. Medical out-of-pocket costs, state continuation and disability-extension premiums are excluded. Certain disability-extension months have different federal limits.
